scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The card is a geographic history of the Dominican Republic and earlier communities in its area, not an assertion that the modern republic existed in 1000 or 1492. The early boundary is an approximate archaeological window. The outline remains unchanged and unverified, and no unverified successor targets are added.

The La Aleta paper was downloaded and its methods, objects, chronology and interpretations read. Recoveries in the cited seasons were controlled underwater surface collections rather than excavations. Basket and gourd dates use published two-sigma ranges, not the narrower intercepts presented in the abstract. The paper’s duho radiocarbon row appears internally inconsistent; no duho date is adopted. A ritual offering interpretation is distinguished from proven intention, and no contents are assigned to the gourd.

Aleta containers illustrate technologies, not a census of household possessions. Preservation under low-oxygen water does not establish that an object will survive recovery. The basket example is the report’s actual conservation experience, not advice to remove archaeological objects.

The Florida Museum’s La Isabela overview and cited publication titles differ in their precise foundation and abandonment wording. The card uses the secure 1490s context and does not repeat all-male or first-European-town superlatives. The warehouse and residence descriptions are site evidence; housing differences are not used to identify particular residents’ wealth or ethnicity.

The hospital’s 1503 beginning and early-sixteenth-century rebuilding are kept distinct. The tourist guide is not evidence for treatment success, equal access or a first-in-the-Americas priority. Its tale of destroyed hospital records during Drake’s attack is not used. The museum house dates from the sixteenth century while the furnishings represent a wealthy nineteenth-century household, not all families or original owners’ possessions.

The civil registration guide is used for record types and incomplete indexing only. Its 1945 beginning claim and its differing earlier dates are not adopted as a national origin date for civil registration. No personal records were searched or published.

The Cocolo account’s mid-nineteenth-century arrival statement is not treated as the date of all labour migration or the founding of a single community. Its older one-remaining-troupe statement and sweeping language-loss claims are omitted. Institutions and repertoire are described historically. Descendants of enslaved people are not labelled enslaved themselves at migration.

The Congos account describes religious practices without treating beliefs as physical facts. Its combined discussion of Pentecost and funerals is not interpreted to mean they are the same event. No exact sixteenth-century founding date is adopted without stronger evidence.

The UNESCO music dates are dates of the cited accounts, not invention dates. The card omits claims of universal participation, a presumed African etymology for bachata and the English source’s confusing four-tempos-per-beat wording. The merengue homework line is plainly a joke about learning movement.

The cassava text draws on the same UNESCO source as the Cuba card. Both passages and source notes were checked together against the per-source summary budget. No incomplete processing or food-safety instructions are given.

The 1999 country study’s historical chapter was read from the Library of Congress PDF. Only selected institutional transitions are adopted. Its opening claim about the first permanent Spanish settlement, inaccurate chronology-table founding date for Santo Domingo, Indigenous demographic assertions, stereotyped racial descriptions and broad judgments about national character are not reproduced. The 1795 treaty transferred a claim; it is not presented as immediate full French control.

The 1492 to 1822 phase deliberately spans several colonial governments and a brief independence declaration, rather than assigning a single sovereign to the whole interval. Eastern Hispaniola’s chronology is distinguished from Haiti’s. Independence in 1844, annexation in 1861, restoration in 1865 and the U.S. occupation in 1916 to 1924 are separate events. The post-1961 phase is broad cultural history, not a single regime or a current-government claim.

Some UNESCO, museum and Library of Congress HTML pages failed on direct opening; their relevant full indexed text was read. The La Aleta and country-study PDFs were downloaded and read, while the government heritage PDF was read through the web reader. No unseen book, image or complete archival collection is claimed as inspected.
The new narrative is author-checked against the cited passages and awaits independent historical review.

identityEvidence.assessment: The outline covers eastern Hispaniola and is consistent with the named Dominican Republic. The imported start in 1878 is map coverage. The distinct hispaniola-spain record includes broader territory, including Puerto Rico, and is not attached to this country card.
